Q6169.L1t: Second-grade number sense work covers reading, writing, comparing and ordering whole numbers up to 1,000.
Q6169.L2t: Base ten blocks come as unit cubes, ten-rods and hundred-flats, and these pieces stand for ones, tens and hundreds.
Q6169.L3t: To build a three-digit number on a place value mat, a student must split it into separate hundreds, tens and ones and show each part with its own blocks.
Q6169.L4t: The lesson best reinforces decomposing quantities, because students break each number into its place value parts.
Q6169.L2f: Base ten blocks were designed mainly to teach fractions and decimals, and they are rarely used for whole numbers.
Q6169.L3f: Each student works alone on a single card and only has to say aloud how many objects the number names, with no comparison to other numbers and no building from parts.
Q6169.L4f: The lesson best reinforces describing quantities, because students are mainly telling how much their number represents.

Q5598.L1t: Hypovolaemic shock is a state of inadequate tissue perfusion caused by low circulating volume, from bleeding or fluid loss.
Q5598.L2t: The body compensates for early blood loss with vasoconstriction and a faster heart rate, which can keep blood pressure steady for a time.
Q5598.L3t: In adults, the first stage of haemorrhage (Class I) covers losses up to roughly 15%, and Class II covers roughly 15 to 30%, with only mild tachycardia and a maintained blood pressure. Clear changes in heart rate and blood pressure therefore appear only after a loss larger than this.
Q5598.L4t: Around thirty percent of blood volume can be lost before heart rate and blood pressure visibly change.
Q5598.L2f: Hypovolaemic shock is defined by a rise in central venous pressure and is mainly caused by failure of the heart pump.
Q5598.L3f: Compensation is exhausted very early, so once a fifth of the blood volume has gone, heart rate rises and blood pressure falls noticeably.
Q5598.L4f: Heart rate and blood pressure begin to change after a loss of about a fifth of blood volume, so that is the answer.

Q8095.L1t: Attachment theory, developed by Bowlby and Ainsworth, describes the emotional bonds that infants form with the people who care for them.
Q8095.L2t: Bowlby described attachment as developing through phases, starting with a pre-attachment phase in the first weeks of life.
Q8095.L3t: In the earliest months infants are still in an indiscriminate phase, so they respond to any adult and do not yet protest at strangers. Preference for particular caregivers and wariness of strangers appear only from about six or seven months.
Q8095.L4t: The youngest infant, a two-month-old girl raised in a safe, stable home, is the one most likely to attach to the unfamiliar male psychologist.
Q8095.L2f: Bowlby argued that infants form attachments only through being fed, and that the process has no sensitive period.
Q8095.L3f: By the end of the first year, infants with mildly inconsistent care have no firmly selective bond, so they accept almost any adult as an attachment figure.
Q8095.L4f: The thirteen-month-old girl with two occasionally neglectful caregivers is the child most likely to attach to the unfamiliar psychologist.
